question: What core problem do subagents in Claude Code solve?

options.text: The cost problem -- subagents are free
options.explanation: Subagents also consume tokens. Their value is in context isolation, not cost savings

options.text: The speed problem -- subagents work faster than the main agent
options.explanation: Subagents aren't faster. Their key advantage is context isolation, not speed

options.text: The context window overflow problem -- each subagent works in an isolated context
options.explanation: A subagent reads files in its own context, produces a brief report, and returns it to the main agent. The main agent's context stays clean

options.text: The security problem -- subagents have no access to files
options.explanation: Subagents do have access to files (via the specified tools). The problem they solve is context overflow

question: Which tool set is correct for a code-review subagent?

options.text: tools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep", "Edit", "Write"] -- with edit rights
options.explanation: A reviewer shouldn't change code -- it analyzes and returns a report. Extra permissions increase the risk of accidental changes

options.text: tools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep", "Edit", "Write", "Bash"] -- full access
options.explanation: Full access for a reviewer violates the principle of least privilege. Read-only tools are enough for a reviewer

options.text: tools: ["Read", "Glob", "Grep"] -- read only
options.explanation: A reviewer should only read code and return a report. Principle of least privilege: don't grant write access to someone who shouldn't write

options.text: Tools don't need to be specified -- the subagent inherits all the main agent's tools
options.explanation: Tools must be specified explicitly. This is a key security mechanism -- restricting what the subagent can do

question: Which model should you choose for a subagent that just searches for files and gathers information?

options.text: The model doesn't affect subagent cost
options.explanation: The model directly affects cost. Haiku is significantly cheaper than Sonnet, and Sonnet is cheaper than Opus

options.text: Opus -- best quality for any task
options.explanation: Opus is overkill for a simple search. Haiku does just as well, but at a much lower cost

options.text: Sonnet -- a universal choice
options.explanation: Sonnet is good for analytical tasks, but for simple file searches Haiku is more economical

options.text: Haiku -- cheap and fast, sufficient for simple tasks
options.explanation: For mechanical tasks (finding files, gathering information), Haiku delivers comparable quality at 20 times lower cost than Opus

question: What does the description parameter in a subagent's frontmatter do?

options.text: It defines the subagent's scope of file access
options.explanation: Access is defined by the tools parameter, not description. Description is for automatic delegation

options.text: It's just a comment for the developer
options.explanation: Description is not a comment, but a functional parameter for automatic task delegation

options.text: It determines when the main agent automatically delegates a task to this subagent
options.explanation: description contains keywords and triggers that let the main agent recognize when a task fits this subagent

options.text: It's displayed in the UI for the user
options.explanation: The primary function of description is to help the main agent decide when to delegate a task

question: What is the difference between foreground and background subagents?

options.text: Foreground has file access, background doesn't
options.explanation: Both types have the same tool access. The difference is in execution synchrony

options.text: Foreground is more expensive because it uses a more powerful model
options.explanation: The model is determined by the model parameter, not the execution mode. Foreground and background can use any model

options.text: Foreground works faster, background works slower
options.explanation: Task execution speed is the same. The difference is whether the main agent waits or continues working

options.text: Foreground: the main agent waits for the result. Background: the subagent works in parallel while the main agent continues
options.explanation: Foreground blocks the main agent until the result is received. Background allows parallel work

question: Why are Git Worktrees needed when working with subagents?

options.text: To save disk space
options.explanation: A worktree creates a separate copy of files, which actually takes up additional space. The goal is isolation, not savings

options.text: For filesystem isolation -- the subagent can freely change files without affecting the main copy
options.explanation: A worktree is a separate working copy of the repository. The subagent experiments in it, while the main code remains untouched

options.text: To speed up file reads by the subagent
options.explanation: Worktrees don't affect read speed. Their purpose is isolating changes

options.text: Worktrees are required for all subagents
options.explanation: Worktrees are only needed for subagents that edit files and whose changes need to be isolated. Read-only agents don't need them

question: You have a task: 'Study the authorization module, find bugs in the API controllers, and write tests.' How should you decompose it correctly?

options.text: Two subagents: one for reading, another for writing
options.explanation: Splitting by operation type (read/write) is less effective than splitting by task. Each subagent should handle one focused task

options.text: No delegation needed -- the main agent can handle it alone
options.explanation: Studying the module, finding bugs, and writing tests involves dozens of files. The main agent's context would overflow. Subagents solve this problem

options.text: One subagent with full permissions and a detailed instruction covering all three tasks
options.explanation: One subagent for three different tasks -- its context will overflow. Decomposition into focused subagents is more effective

options.text: Three subagents: researcher to study, reviewer to find bugs, test-writer for tests
options.explanation: Each subagent gets a focused task. This is more effective than one subagent with a huge assignment -- the context doesn't overflow

question: Why is it important to specify a response format in a subagent's instructions?

options.text: A structured response saves the main agent's context, which doesn't have to spend it parsing an arbitrary format
options.explanation: The subagent's result is returned to the main agent. A clear format (file:line → description) is easy to parse and takes up less context

options.text: A format is only needed for background subagents
options.explanation: The response format matters for any subagent -- both foreground and background. It's a matter of context savings and predictability

options.text: Without a format the subagent can't return a response
options.explanation: The subagent will return a response regardless. But without a format, the response can be verbose and unstructured

options.text: A response format is mandatory -- without it there will be an error
options.explanation: The format isn't technically mandatory, but it's very important for quality. Without it, the response is unpredictable

options.text: The subagent gets a copy of the main agent's context and works in isolation -- changes don't affect the main agent
options.explanation: fork creates a copy (fork) of the current context. The subagent sees the conversation history, but its context is isolated from the main agent's

options.text: The subagent runs in a separate operating system process
options.explanation: fork is about the conversation context (message history), not OS processes

options.text: The subagent has no access to the conversation history
options.explanation: The opposite is true: fork provides a copy of the context. The subagent sees the history, but its work doesn't pollute the main agent's context

options.text: The subagent creates a fork of the Git repository
options.explanation: context: fork refers to the conversation context, not Git. Worktrees are used for file isolation

question: Three researcher subagents (Haiku) are launched in parallel in the background. What happens?

options.text: Only one subagent can work in the background at a time

options.text: The main agent pauses until all three finish
options.explanation: That describes foreground mode. In background mode the main agent continues working in parallel

options.text: Each explores its own part of the codebase simultaneously, and the main agent continues the dialogue with the user
options.explanation: Background subagents work in parallel. This is the most powerful pattern -- instead of reading 150 files sequentially, three agents work at the same time

options.text: They work sequentially -- first the first one, then the second, then the third
options.explanation: Background subagents work in parallel, not sequentially. That's their key advantage

question: When is a worktree NOT needed for a subagent?

options.text: When the subagent uses the Haiku model
options.explanation: The model doesn't affect whether a worktree is needed. What matters is whether the subagent will change files

options.text: A worktree is always needed for security
